claim: Trenches: the Pacific rim has long narrow curving trenches thousands of km long and 8 to 10 km deep, made by subduction; e.g. the Nazca Plate subducts beneath South America along the Peru-Chile trench, raising the Andes

claim: Subduction zones have deep-ocean trenches, shallow-to-deep earthquakes and mountain ranges with active volcanoes; e.g. the Aleutians, Alaska and the north-west US coast. USGS also says only under 10 per cent of earthquakes occur within plate interiors
source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Earthquakes', Where Earthquakes Occur
note: This is the 'why a belt, not scatter' point: most earthquakes sit on plate boundaries. Old (1990s) publication; the 10% is USGS's own wording.

claim: Wadati-Benioff zone: the inclined line of earthquake foci from shallow (0-70 km) through intermediate (70-300 km) to deep (over 300 km); volcanoes are frequently above the 100 km depth contour
source: USGS ComCat event usp000ba6g (M 7.7 Fiji region, 19 Aug 2002), Tectonic Summary
note: Explains why the belt has volcano line behind the trench. The page is about the 2002 Fiji quake; it is a general USGS definition.

claim: Deep earthquakes: two M 7.7 quakes in the Tonga-Fiji subduction zone on 19 August 2002 struck at 580 km and 675 km depth, near the bottom limit of global earthquakes; the Pacific plate subducts there at about 75 mm per year; 35 other events above M 7.5 have been recorded in the area since 1900
source: USGS ComCat event usp000ba6g (M 7.7 Fiji region, 19 Aug 2002), Tectonic Summary
note: Plate convergence 50-90 mm/yr per the same page. NCERT Class XI (ledger V026 source) also says rim-of-Pacific quakes are deep-seated, mid-ocean-ridge ones shallow.

claim: NCERT Class XI: earthquake foci at the mid-oceanic ridges are shallow, but along the Alpine-Himalayan belt and the rim of the Pacific the earthquakes are deep-seated; the Pacific rim is called the rim of fire because of its active volcanoes
